newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - UK POLITICS. RUSSIA.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - UK POLITICS. RUSSIA.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

As UK politicians strive to attract wavering voters in the last few hours before Britain goes to the polls, it is interesting to speculate whether UK insurers have been swayed from their traditional support for the conservatives.

A survey of annual reports in a recent UK trade magazine indicates that listed insurers and brokers have been cutting back their donations to the Conservative Party and associated bodies, but even so they have donated 1.3 million stg during the current parliament and 5.3 million stg since 1979.
This compares to donations of only 74,000 stg to the Labour and Liberal Democratic parties.
Top Tory backers were Royal & SunAlliance, which has donated 1.1 million stg since 1979, Hambros, which shelled out 824,250 and Guardian Royal Exchange, which paid funds of 758,198.

Insurance broking firms were the most prolific, with Sedgwick, Willis Corroon, Steel Burrill Jones, CE Heath, and having donated a total of 1.36 million stg to the Tories since 1979 Sun Life donated 15,000 stg to the SDP Liberal Alliance between 1984 and 1986 and showed a payment of 10,000 stg to the Labour Party in its 1995 accounts.
This was the only payment made to Labour, suggesting it might be too early to claim the party has won over the city with its charm offensive.

But figures for many insurers show a decline in contributions since the current Conservative term of office. Sedgwick, which from 1979 made annual donations of between 10,000 and 20,000 stg, has not donated since 1993. Even stalwart backer Hambros only donated 56 000 stg last year, compared with 104,000 stg in 1995.

Future backing from recently merged Royal & Sun Alliance is uncertain. Royal quit funding the Conservatives in 1989, while Sun Alliance has made donations of 35,000 to 50,000 stg every year since 1985.
If the political party controlling the economy of Britain changes hands tomorrow, the economies of Britain's political parties might change too.
--OO0OO--

Last week, the All-Russian Insurance Union told insurers to increase their minimum authorised capital to 10 billion roubles. At the moment, only around 12 percent of insurance companies have more than one billion roubles authorised capital.

Yesterday, the head of the country's insurance supervisory body warned that the "critical situation (within the industry) is continuing to deepen." The supervisory body has withdrawn 12 licences and is considering the situation of a further 30 companies.

Fewer new companies are being set up and the signs are that, after a burst of activity after economic liberalisation, the industry is embarking on a period of consolidation. Two hundred of the country's 2,500 insurers recorded no activity in the first quarter.

While the number of companies may decline and the short term outlook remains uncertain, the long term growth prospects for Russia are good. The challenge for western insurers looking for opportunities to do business in Russia is to identify the handful of companies who will be the big players of the future.
